title: The Lie About Guilt We Don't Question in Business
author: Summer Mulder
summary: Mulder interrogates a belief she says goes unquestioned in business — that feeling guilty is proof of being good — and dismantles it from her own experience as a leader. For years she treated her guilt over bad calls, overpromises, and projects that went sideways as evidence that she cared and was therefore responsible, empathetic, and 'better' somehow. Sitting with it, she reframes guilt as self-absorption rather than virtue: it is a spotlight pointed inward, keeping the focus on her own remorse and internal spiral instead of on the people who needed clarity, leadership, and action from her. In practice, she argues, guilt made her hesitant, self-doubting, and less available, eroding trust at exactly the moments her team needed her steady. Her pivot is a single reframing question: if a team member, a child, or a close friend made the same mistake she punishes herself for, she would recognize the risk and pressure they were under and forgive them — so why treat her own guilt as virtuous when it only keeps her small and unavailable? The piece ends by proposing that guilt may be less a sign of goodness than a way of avoiding becoming the person the next chapter requires.
points: Mulder names the unexamined equation at the heart of the piece — 'we mistake feeling guilty for being good' — and identifies it as especially entrenched in business, where remorse is read as proof of care and responsibility.
Her core reframe is that guilt is self-focused rather than virtuous: a spotlight pointed inward that centers the leader's own remorse instead of the clarity, leadership, and action owed to others.
She makes the leadership cost concrete: guilt made her hesitant, prone to second-guessing, and less available, eroding trust precisely when her team needed her steady.

The unlocking device is a perspective-swap question — whether she would forgive a team member, child, or friend for the same mistake she punishes in herself — which exposes the double standard and the risk-taking that guilt discounts.
The closing move recasts guilt as avoidance rather than conscience: instead of proving goodness, it can be a way of not becoming the person the next chapter requires.
quotes: We mistake feeling guilty for being good. Especially in business.
Guilt didn’t make me show up better. It made me disappear. It made me hesitant.
Guilt is a spotlight. And the spotlight is pointed inward. It doesn’t fix the situation.
It just keeps you in a loop where everything is about your feelings instead of the responsibility in front of you.
If someone on your team came to you with the same mistake you’re punishing yourself for… would you forgive them?
What if guilt isn’t proof you’re a good person or a good leader? What if it’s a way of avoiding becoming the person the next chapter requires?
